source.title: Batch Normalization is a Cause of Adversarial Vulnerability
source.authors: A. Galloway; A. Golubeva; T. Tanay; M. Moussa; Graham W. Taylor

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper and appendices; no truncation or garbling apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The paper compares training and trainability across batch-normalization settings and reports training outcomes, using different measures from the versions’ main benchmark claims.
record.gate_note: Most experiments measure test robustness, not training classification error or training speed, so those results are not rows. The paper also discusses prior work on normalization, optimization, and initialization; cited results are not rows.
record.test_reason: Own training results bear on V1 and V6: CIFAR-10 WideResNets fit their training set, MNIST networks converge faster with batch normalization, and Adversarial Spheres networks show the opposite learning-rate tolerance. The latter extends the normalization comparison to a new setting.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate but incomplete. The authors conclude that accelerated training and occasional clean-accuracy gains from batch normalization come with reduced robustness. They also conclude that vulnerability need not inherently scale with input dimension, and report less stable training with batch normalization on Adversarial Spheres.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies batch normalization’s effect on robustness and trainability; it does not reproduce the cited studies’ training-error or normalization comparisons as stated in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Learning rate and batch size affect trainability in the MNIST depth experiments; the Adversarial Spheres batch-normalized network is sensitive to learning rate.

fits_no_version.finding: Batch normalization generally reduces robustness to adversarial perturbations and noise, and weight decay can remove the observed dependence of vulnerability on input dimension.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Normalization and regularization choices affect robustness to input perturbations.

record.problems: The CIFAR-10 training-fit statement is aggregate across the two WideResNet variants and gives no numerical training error. The Adversarial Spheres trainability results give no exact error values; the figure shows confidence intervals without numerical summaries.
record.rows_left_out: No test-robustness rows were included because the versions concern training error, trainability, initialization, learning-rate stability, or training speed. MNIST depth plots report test accuracy rather than the training outcomes named in these versions.

untested.parts: CIFAR-100, corrupted or random labels, capacity dependence, early stopping, optimizer comparisons, and systematic regularization effects.
Teacher-student ReLU optimization, spurious minima, and the effect of extra student neurons.
Matched plain versus identity-shortcut convolutional networks and their training-error degradation; very deep tanh initialization and normalization-free Fixup training.
Comparisons between initialization schemes establishing their effects on training speed or trainable depth.
Initial linearized stability thresholds, curvature trajectories, catapult recovery, and edge-of-stability dynamics.

Quantified speed comparisons on the specified sigmoid, VGG, and Inception architectures; controlled maximum-learning-rate comparisons on those architectures; Fixup matching normalization's speed and stability without any normalization.

missing.what: Qualitative convergence-speed comparison: unnormalized MNIST networks took longer to converge, leading the authors to extend training from 10 to 40 epochs. Record this without treating those durations as a measured fourfold speedup.
missing.locator: Figure 2 caption; Appendix A.5 and Figure 5

missing.what: Explicit MNIST trainability outcomes beyond the test-accuracy heatmaps: batch normalization imposes a batch-size-dependent depth ceiling near 40 layers; unnormalized models can train deeper. Some unnormalized 55–60-layer configurations fail at large batch sizes but become trainable after reducing the learning rate.
missing.locator: Section 3 discussion of Figure 2; Figure 2 caption; Appendix A.5

record.verdict_notes: This study is not an original source for these versions. Adversarial Spheres fitting does not bear on V1's convolutional CIFAR claim. The Fixup experiment cannot establish normalization-free training because its implementation retains one batch-normalization layer. Robustness costs do not themselves limit V6, which makes no robustness guarantee.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test CIFAR-100, corrupted or random labels, SGD versus Adam, smaller models, early stopping, or regularized recipes generally.

Does not compare training speed as parameter updates to a fixed accuracy on the named MNIST/CIFAR-10/ImageNet architectures, or test Fixup’s training speed against normalization. The Fixup comparison reports fitting by 150 epochs but not relative speed.

rows.subject: Two-hidden-layer ReLU network, unnormalized
